title: The first forests
summary: The origin of trees and forests in the Mid Devonian, 393 to 383 million years ago, was a turning point in Earth history, with permanent changes to land ecology, geochemical cycles, atmospheric carbon dioxide and climate. At Cairo, New York, scientists found the root systems of a 385-million-year-old forest. One researcher says the world has never been the same since.

uncertainty.note: Stein et al. (2020) date the Middle Devonian emergence of forests to 393–383 Ma (Eifelian–Givetian), with the Cairo paleosol rooted horizon specifically dated to c. 385 Ma, preceding the c. 382–380 Ma Gilboa forest.

as_recorded.value: 385-million-year old trees that existed during the Devonian Period
origin of trees and forests in the Mid Devonian (393-383 Ma)

where.modern_name: Cairo, New York, United States (early fossil forest)
where.historical_name: Catskill delta complex, Euramerica (Laurussia); Middle Devonian floodplain

importance.justification: The spread of Earth's first forests revolutionized continental weathering, drew down atmospheric carbon dioxide, created deep soils, and permanently reshaped global biogeochemical cycles.

related.because: The initial colonization of land by non-vascular embryophytes provided the phylogenetic foundation from which arborescent lignophytes evolved.
Canopy forests created complex terrestrial microclimates, leaf litter soils, and food sources that facilitated tetrapod and arthropod terrestrialization.
Intensified root weathering accelerated nutrient runoff into epicontinental seas, triggering widespread oceanic eutrophication, anoxia, and mass extinction.
